description: We're taking on the Mars mapping challenge: building a layered, interactive map that combines data from multiple NASA missions to help astronauts plan and carry out a Marswalk. Our strengths are software development, math, physics, and data analysis, plus experience doing real research with astronomical data.
summary:
Google Maps tells you how to get there. On Mars, on foot, what matters is whether you can get back.

Jezero Marswalk is a layered map of a 21-kilometre square of Jezero crater, centred on the habitat, and a planner for walking it. MRO’s HiRISE elevation, MRO’s CRISM detections of probable carbonate, olivine and clay, and Mars Odyssey’s THEMIS thermal inertia, which flags likely loose ground, sit on one 5-metre grid.

Every walkable cell becomes a node linked to its neighbours. Edges are directed, because climbing costs more than descending, and weighted by the time a step takes or the suit supply it consumes, turning walking into a shortest-path problem.

Out of that come the fastest and most economical routes to each mineral detection and back, and the trade-offs between them; tours that fit the hours available; and an emergency mode showing which shelters, radio-contact points and the habitat remain reachable on remaining supply, keeping a quarter in reserve.

Getting back matters most. On our 28 routes, no point is more than 7.5 minutes’ walk, at 3.6 km/h on flat ground, from the habitat or a ridge that blocks part of the sky, and part of the radiation with it.
details:
HOW IT WORKS

Jezero Marswalk plans walks for an astronaut on foot in Jezero crater and reports

whether the walk back fits in what is left of the suit supply. The app is at

marseva.us, for Mars EVA.

It combines four NASA missions and eight data products: MRO (HiRISE elevation, CRISM

mineral detections), Mars Odyssey (THEMIS thermal inertia), Mars 2020 (Perseverance's

traverse, Mastcam-Z and Navcam imagery, MEDA pressure) and MSL (Curiosity's RAD

radiation record).

The first three are resampled onto one grid. Ground east distance is corrected by

cos(latitude), 0.948 at Jezero, so a cell is 4.74 m east by 5.0 m north. The grid is

4,280 by 4,297 cells, covering 20.3 by 21.5 km. Roughness is the standard deviation of

the 1 m slopes inside each cell, which keeps rough ground from being flattened by

averaging, though a HiRISE terrain model resolves detail coarser than its 1 m posting,

so boulders of a metre or two stay invisible to it.

That ground becomes a graph. Every walkable cell is a node joined to its 8 neighbours

and, where the ground allows, the 8 knight moves as well: 16 headings rather than 8.

An 8-connected grid can only travel in multiples of 45 degrees, so a route to a point

on an intermediate bearing is a staircase up to 8.2% longer than the straight line; 16

headings bring that to 2.7%. A knight move spans two cells and is priced from its ends,

so it is only an edge where the cells it passes over are walkable and sit within 0.5 m

of the straight line between them. Without that guard it would fly over a one-cell

ridge for free. The routes in this submission use a 3 by 3 km window around the

habitat: about 333,000 walkable cells and 5.0 million directed edges. Edges are

directed because climbing costs more than descending.

Each edge carries two weights. Time comes from Tobler's hiking function, scaled so

flat ground gives 3.6 km/h, the walk-back speed the Apollo planners used. Effort comes

from Pandolf's metabolic equation with a terrain factor from roughness and thermal

inertia, reported as hours of suit supply at the 1200 BTU/h EVA planning rate. That is

a change of units, not of ranking, but hours are the budget an EVA is actually planned

against. Standing at a science stop consumes supply too: Pandolf with V = 0 leaves only

the standing term, exactly half the flat walking rate, so the stops are counted rather

than ignored.

A step across a hillside splits the terrain's steepest slope into the grade along the

direction of travel and the side slope across it, tan(terrain)^2 = tan(grade)^2 +

tan(side)^2. Side slope is where falls happen and neither Tobler nor Pandolf models it:

both were measured walking straight up or down. We measure it on every route and

segment, and add half of it to the grade Pandolf sees.

Dijkstra then returns the optimal route for that grid and that cost model. Minimising

time gives the fastest route, minimising effort the most economical. Sweeping a blend

gives non-dominated alternatives, though a linear sweep reaches only the convex hull of

the trade-off curve, so these are the non-dominated routes that sweep finds, not the

complete Pareto front.

The published outputs are 30 routes, 4 emergency scenarios, 13 waypoints, 16 mineral

patches and 8 map layers. The full tour of all six science stops is 2.71 km and

3 h 58 min: 58 minutes walking and three hours of science, inside the 6 h recommended

EVA, for 3.13 h of suit supply, 39% of an 8 h suit.

Shelters are walkable cells where the terrain hides the most sky, measured from horizon

angles over 500 m in 16 directions. The six we found hide 18.3 to 21.4 percent of the

sky. Our model scales radiation dose by that fraction, which assumes a uniformly bright

sky; because the hidden sky sits near the horizon, where radiation crosses more

atmosphere, the real saving is at most that fraction. These are partial shelters, not

safe rooms. Communication points are walkable cells with line of sight to a 3 m antenna

at the habitat, with the suit antenna at 1.8 m. No point on any published route is more

than 7.2 minutes from the habitat or a shelter, or 12.4 minutes from the habitat alone.

Each science stop also carries real Perseverance photographs, Mastcam-Z and Navcam,

taken from the nearest rover position 48 to 294 m away, and the surface pressure MEDA

measured there.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

Python 3.10 and 3.13. NumPy and SciPy for the grid and the search

(scipy.sparse.csgraph.dijkstra), rasterio for the rasters, cdflib for the RAD CDF

files, Pillow and matplotlib for the map layers. FastAPI and uvicorn for the routing

API, pytest for 56 tests (16 engine, 40 API), Docker for Cloud Run, GitHub Actions for

continuous integration. The front end was built on Base44. No special hardware: the

full export runs in about 12 seconds in roughly 470 MB of RAM, and the API answers a

route in about 0.3 seconds.

Code, data and documentation: https://github.com/MiguelJM17/jezero-marswalk

Live app: https://marseva.us

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Walkback distance limited where Apollo crews could go, and Mars tightens two things the

Moon did not. Gravity is 0.38 g against the Moon's 0.17 g, so every step costs more.

And a one-way signal takes 4 to 24 minutes, so the decision about whether to press on

or turn back is made on Mars, without Earth, with whatever the map told the crew before

they left.

The decision they need is not the shortest line. It is which of several real options

fits the supply, the time and the risk they will accept, and what happens if something

fails halfway.

The direct user group is small: EVA planners for missions that do not yet exist. We do

not claim mass impact. What we claim is that the method is reusable. The engine knows

nothing about Jezero; it reads a raster and builds a graph. Point it at another digital

terrain model, with that site's own constants, and it produces the same analysis for

another place.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Least-cost path over a terrain grid is a known technique. Four choices are ours.

First, we do not return one route. We return the non-dominated alternatives, so the

astronaut sees the trade-off instead of a single answer chosen for them by a weighting

they never saw.

Second, the walk back is part of the route, not an afterthought. Every route is a round

trip, every emergency answer keeps a 25 percent reserve, and every route reports its

worst-case distance from safety.

Third, shelter is computed from terrain geometry: how much sky a cell hides, and

whether the habitat antenna can see it. Those two layers add where to hide and where to

call for help to a terrain map.

Fourth, we price what the standard equations leave out. Side slope is not in Tobler or

Pandolf, so we derive it from the geometry and penalise it, and the result is routes

that are both safer and shorter than the ones we started with.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

We decided early that a map which hides risk is worse than no map, so slopes above 20

degrees produce a warning, never a removed route. The carbonate routes still cross

ground above 20 degrees, and we report how much.

We made downhill never cheaper than flat in the effort weight. The clamp sets the grade

to zero going down; the rate can still fall below flat because the speed term shrinks,

but the effort of a step never falls below that of a flat step of the same length,

which we checked by sweeping the grades. That holds because Tobler lengthens the time

enough to compensate, not because of the clamp.

We separated what we know from what we assumed. routing/config.py holds 29 constants,

each marked SOURCED with its reference or ASSUMPTION with its reason. Minerals are

always "probable", never confirmed. Oxygen figures are flagged as unverified. The

radiation figure was measured by Curiosity in Gale crater, not Jezero, and we label it

that way.

We know the gaps. Pandolf was measured on Earth, at 1 g, without a spacesuit, and we

have not corrected it for 0.38 g. Both equations are applied outside the grades they

were measured on. The side-slope weight is ours: no measurement exists for a suited

astronaut traversing a Martian hillside, so we measured what the weight changes instead

of arguing for it, and the benefit arrives at 0.25 and then flattens, which means the

conclusion does not depend on the number. The penalty also lives only in the effort

weight, because Pandolf is where a grade term exists and Tobler has none, so the

fastest route still accepts side slope and only reports it. Multi-stop ordering is an

exact exhaustive search, fine for six stops and factorial beyond roughly ten. The app's

trip log records the route an astronaut chose but not yet what actually happened, which

is the measurement that would replace those assumptions with data.

VALIDATION, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE

We compared our routes with Perseverance's real drives, sols 401 to 762. Between 56 and

100 percent of each route stays within 100 m of the rover's path. On its own that proves

nothing, because we chose stops near the rover's path. So we measured the baseline: a

straight line from the habitat to the same stop, ignoring terrain entirely. It scores

83.3 percent against our routes' 80.3 percent.

A straight line does slightly better. The honest reading is that this is a sanity check,

not a validation of route quality: our routes stay mostly inside the corridor

Perseverance actually crossed.

The same script measures side slope, and that comparison is the one we would act on.

Perseverance's own path inside this window reaches 21.0 degrees of ground slope, 10 m of

it above 20, and a maximum side slope of 17.7 degrees with not one metre above 20. A

six-wheeled vehicle with a far wider stance than a person stayed inside 20 degrees of

cross-slope everywhere it went here. It chose its path for science and wheel safety

rather than human effort, so this bounds the question rather than settling it, but it is

the only traverse of this terrain that has happened. Pricing side slope brought the

exposure across all our routes from 570 m above 20 degrees down to 171 m, and the routes

got shorter at the same time.

Both tables are reproducible: docs/validation/baseline_check.py.

USE OF AI TOOLS

We used AI tools in four ways, all directed and checked by the team. Anthropic's Claude

helped write and debug the Python processing and routing code, process and cross-check

the NASA data files, draft the repository documentation, and edit the text of this

submission. OpenAI Codex helped build an earlier data adapter. Base44, an AI app

builder, generated the front-end code at marseva.us; we specified the behaviour and the

data files it reads.

What the AI did not do: the project idea, the challenge choice, the site, the six

science stops and every modelling decision are the team's. No AI generated or

synthesised any data. Every number in the outputs comes from running this code on the

NASA products listed in the README. Rover photos, positions and the validation were

selected and checked by the team.
